input:
This executive summary looks at a possible heat-recovery retrofit at a food plant and at whether the project should move forward at this stage. The plant currently uses 2591 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration, which is a substantial part of the overall picture being considered here. According to the equipment vendor, the retrofit is projected to save 16% of that electricity use, which works out to a derived saving of 415 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost of the retrofit is $412k. Using an electricity price of $0.13 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $54k, and the derived simple payback is 7.6 years.

It is important to note, however, that the saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant, and furthermore that the refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, so there are real questions about how the projected saving would translate into practice. The recommendation is therefore that a metered trial should be carried out on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision is made, with the plant engineer owning the trial, so that the eventual decision can be based on evidence gathered at the plant itself rather than on the projection alone.
target:
The recommendation is a metered trial of the heat-recovery retrofit on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial.

The plant uses 2591 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. The equipment vendor projects that the retrofit would save 16% of that use, a derived saving of 415 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost is $412k. At an electricity price of $0.13 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $54k and the derived simple payback is 7.6 years. The payback is shorter than in many such cases, and it still rests entirely on the projected percentage: the capital cost and the electricity price are stated figures, while the saving that drives both derived quantities is not.

The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant. Refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, so the annual projection pairs a measured annual total with a percentage that no measurement at this plant supports, across a load profile whose peak month is missing. A metered trial on one line measures the saving where the retrofit would actually work, and the decision that follows can be taken on a measured percentage and a recomputed payback, rather than on the vendor figure carried through the arithmetic. The cost of the trial is the cost of metering one line, and it is incurred before the capital decision, not after it.
